Although our environmental risk management includes efforts to address weather-related disruptions, changes in natural resource conditions can affect operations through mechanisms that are not limited to greenhouse gas emissions. For example, extreme heat and changing precipitation patterns can increase demand for process water and reduce available supply in our service areas. In addition, higher river temperatures and altered seasonal flow can impact the ability of nearby utilities to provide industrial water within specification.

Our reliance on regional infrastructure means that interruptions in water supply or quality can occur even when our own equipment is functioning properly. We may be required to curtail operations, adjust production schedules, or invest in additional water treatment capacity. Such measures could require permits and engineering work, and may not be completed quickly.

Natural resource conditions can also influence land stability. Increased runoff and soil moisture variability may elevate the risk of slope failures or undermining at sites built on marginal foundations. If this occurs, remediation and stabilization could be expensive and would likely delay projects and capital expenditures.

We cannot assure you that disruptions related to water and land conditions will not occur or that our mitigation efforts will be sufficient to protect our business from material impacts to operations, costs, or customer service levels.
label: Natural Capital
generation_notes: Water supply/quality via altered flow/temperature and land stability/slope failures; avoids explicit decarbonization/regulation framing.

risk_heading: Water Supply and Water Quality Constraints
paragraph_text:
We rely on a combination of municipal and industrial water sources to operate our manufacturing sites, perform processing activities, and support research and development. Many of our facilities are located in regions that have experienced periodic droughts, tightening of surface-water allocations, or restrictions on withdrawals during dry seasons. In addition, stricter discharge requirements can limit our ability to treat wastewater and reuse process water at historical rates or costs. If drought conditions persist, if regulators curtail withdrawals, or if water quality deteriorates due to upstream contamination or extreme weather events, we may experience production slowdowns, increased operating costs, or the need to incur capital expenditures to install additional treatment capacity, alternative sourcing arrangements, or water-efficiency equipment.

Even where we have contingency plans, supply interruptions or inability to meet permitted water-quality thresholds could lead to enforcement actions, higher fees, or temporary shutdowns. Any of these outcomes could materially and adversely affect our results of operations, financial condition, and ability to meet customer demand.

risk_heading: Biodiversity and Ecosystem Impacts from Sourcing and Operations
paragraph_text:
Certain components and raw materials we procure depend on ecosystems that are sensitive to land-use changes and habitat disruption. Expansion of agricultural production, deforestation, and degradation of wetlands or other habitats in sourcing regions could affect the availability, quality, and cost of materials we use. In some cases, environmental conditions such as changes in soil composition, pollinator populations, or local water regimes may reduce yields or require longer processing times, which can create supply bottlenecks. 

We are also subject to increasing scrutiny from customers and regulators regarding biodiversity protection and responsible land management, including requirements that certain suppliers demonstrate traceability and compliance with land-use and conservation standards. If we are unable to obtain required documentation, if key suppliers are impacted by environmental restrictions, or if adverse ecosystem effects lead to interruptions in procurement or increased regulatory burdens, our operating results could be negatively affected.

To mitigate these risks, we work with suppliers on improved environmental practices and monitor supply continuity, but we cannot guarantee that these efforts will fully prevent disruptions or cost increases.

risk_heading: Land Use, Soil Conditions, and Site Remediation Costs
paragraph_text:
Our operations involve the use, storage, and handling of materials on properties that may be subject to soil and groundwater investigations, permitting constraints, and remediation obligations. Over time, historic activities by us or prior owners, spills, leaks, or natural processes could result in contamination in soil or groundwater and necessitate remediation under applicable environmental laws. Even when contamination is localized, regulators may require investigations and long-term monitoring, which could delay expansions or limit permissible use of portions of a site.

Remediation requirements can be costly and uncertain as the scope of contamination, identification of responsible parties, and effectiveness of remediation methods may not be known until investigative studies are completed. Additionally, changes in regulatory standards or cleanup technologies could increase the cost or duration of required remediation activities. If we incur remediation expenses beyond what we currently reserve, or if remediation prevents us from using a site as intended, our financial results and operational flexibility may be adversely impacted.

We maintain policies and controls designed to reduce environmental incidents; however, the occurrence of an environmental condition and the associated remediation obligations are inherently difficult to predict.

risk_heading: Supply Disruptions Due to Land Degradation and Resource Scarcity
paragraph_text:
We purchase certain agricultural inputs and fiber-based materials that can be affected by land degradation, declining soil fertility, and erosion. Overuse of land by suppliers, unsustainable farming practices, or insufficient nutrient management can reduce yields and increase volatility in the cost and availability of these inputs. Additionally, resource scarcity—such as limited irrigation capacity or deteriorating local water conditions—can constrain production and cause suppliers to shift to alternative crops or regions.

Because some of our supply relationships are concentrated among a limited number of producers, any deterioration in the underlying land resource base could result in shortages, delays in shipments, or substitutions that do not meet our specifications. Meeting quality requirements may require additional processing steps or alternative sourcing agreements, which could increase operating costs. 

Regulatory and customer expectations regarding sustainable land management and traceability are also increasing. If land remediation obligations or compliance requirements are imposed on our suppliers, they may pass through costs or face disruptions that affect our delivery schedules. While we attempt to diversify sourcing and incorporate sustainability criteria, we cannot assure that land degradation will not adversely affect our business.

risk_heading: Regulatory Action Concerning Natural Habitat Conservation
paragraph_text:
From time to time, we may need to acquire or develop property and infrastructure to support growth and maintain existing operations. Proposed projects can require environmental review and permitting that may include evaluation of impacts to protected habitats, wetlands, and threatened or endangered species. If our sites or expansion plans are located near sensitive ecological areas, permitting may take longer than expected or require design changes to avoid or mitigate habitat impacts.

In certain jurisdictions, regulators may impose mitigation obligations, including restoration, creation of comparable habitat, or restrictions on land use that could reduce buildable area or increase construction costs. Delays can also result if there are disputes with local stakeholders or if protected species are identified in project areas. Such delays and additional mitigation requirements could adversely affect our capital expenditure timing and the ability to expand capacity.

We attempt to address permitting risks through early site assessments and environmental consultants; however, the regulatory process is uncertain and could result in adverse outcomes that impact our operations and results of operations.

risk_heading: Impact of Extreme Weather on Coastal and Riverine Operations
paragraph_text:
Some of our facilities, storage areas, and logistics routes are located near coastal zones or along waterways. Storm surges, river flooding, and saltwater intrusion can damage physical assets, affect access to water-dependent operations, and disrupt the availability of feedstocks transported by barge or other waterborne means. These events can also affect the quality of raw materials and process water, including increasing salinity beyond design tolerances.

In response to recurring extreme weather, infrastructure providers and regulators may revise water management rules, impose new stormwater permitting requirements, or require protective upgrades. These changes could require significant capital expenditures to reinforce structures, raise equipment, or modify intake systems and storage practices.

Moreover, damage to surrounding ecosystems from extreme events can create additional compliance obligations, such as restoration requirements or limitations on certain activities during sensitive seasons for aquatic species. If we are unable to maintain uninterrupted operations or incur unplanned capital costs, our results of operations could be adversely affected.

We have taken measures to improve resilience, but the timing, severity, and frequency of extreme weather events remain difficult to predict.

risk_heading: Water Reuse Limitations and Treatment Capacity Constraints
paragraph_text:
Our manufacturing process is designed to use certain quantities of recycled water, but regulatory limits on discharge, cooling-water chemistry, and water-quality parameters may restrict how much we can reuse. As permits are renewed, regulators may require more stringent standards for treated water or impose caps on the volume of water that can be withdrawn from local sources. These changes could reduce the effectiveness of our water-reuse systems and require us to draw additional water from alternative supplies.

If we are required to increase fresh-water intake, we may face higher utility costs, longer lead times to secure alternative supplies, or greater operational risk during drought. In addition, increasing treatment capacity or upgrading water-reuse equipment typically requires engineering time and significant investment. Delays in construction, procurement of specialized equipment, or commissioning can impact production schedules.

We monitor water usage and maintain our systems, but there can be no assurance that future permit renewals will allow continued reliance on existing water-recycling practices or that we will be able to implement upgrades on a timely basis. Any interruption or increased cost could have a material adverse effect on our business.

risk_heading: Risks Associated with Extractive Resource Depletion at Supplier Sites
paragraph_text:
Some of our upstream suppliers depend on extractive activities such as quarrying, mining, or drilling to produce materials used in our products. Over time, these operations can experience depletion of economically recoverable reserves, changes in local environmental conditions, or increasing restrictions related to water availability and land access. Such issues may shorten supply lifecycles and reduce the reliability of material delivery.

If a supplier's permitted extraction area is reduced, if water used in processing becomes unavailable due to allocation rules, or if environmental remediation obligations increase, the supplier may be forced to scale back operations or change production methods. These changes can lead to quality variability and increased costs for raw materials, which could require us to adjust specifications, increase inspection activities, or find alternative suppliers.

In addition, competitors may seek similar resources, intensifying pricing volatility. If we cannot secure alternative supplies on acceptable terms, or if the quality of replacement materials does not meet our requirements, our ability to manufacture products and meet customer demand could be impaired.

While we maintain multi-sourcing strategies for certain materials, the risks associated with depletion and environmental constraints remain outside our direct control.

Any material remediation expense, whether unexpected or greater than our reserves, could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.

risk_heading: Risks from Regulatory Changes on Water and Wetlands Permitting
paragraph_text:
Our facilities and projects involve work near streams, drainage channels, or wetlands, which can require permits and approvals under federal, state, and local programs. Regulatory agencies periodically change permitting processes, mitigation requirements, and standards for evaluating impacts to aquatic resources. These changes can increase the time and cost required to obtain approvals for maintenance, expansions, or infrastructure upgrades.

For example, regulators may require additional mitigation credits, impose stricter timing restrictions tied to spawning or migration seasons, or require enhanced monitoring of restored areas. If we cannot obtain permits within required timeframes, or if modifications are necessary to comply with new conditions, our ability to complete projects and operate as planned could be delayed.

In addition, if wetlands or water resources near our sites are reclassified or determined to be more sensitive than previously concluded, regulators may revoke or limit existing permits. Any such outcomes could trigger compliance-related costs, production disruptions, or claims by counterparties.

We seek to anticipate permitting risks through environmental studies and ongoing stakeholder engagement; however, changes in regulatory standards are not under our control.

risk_heading: Heat, Drought, and Cooling Water Availability

Certain operations use cooling water and require stable water availability to maintain equipment temperatures and ensure safe process performance. During periods of drought, regulators may impose restrictions on water withdrawals and on the temperature of water discharged back into the environment. Higher ambient temperatures can further increase cooling water demand and reduce the capacity of nearby water bodies to absorb heat.

If we face limitations on withdrawals or discharge temperatures, we may need to reduce production rates, operate alternative cooling methods that may be less efficient, or invest in additional cooling capacity and water-supply infrastructure. These measures can be expensive and may not be completed quickly enough to prevent operational disruptions.

The risk may be amplified where multiple industrial users draw from the same water sources or where water bodies are subject to ecological constraints. In those situations, curtailment decisions can be outside our control. Delays or reduced output could adversely affect our ability to fulfill customer orders and may result in higher operating costs.

While we manage water usage and maintain monitoring systems, future heat and drought conditions could create material adverse impacts to our operations.

In certain operating regions, seasonal shifts and hydrologic variability can change wastewater volumes and affect treatment reliability. Additionally, constraints on water sources can limit the availability of process water needed for treatment chemicals and equipment operation.

If we experience conditions that reduce system efficiency—such as insufficient water levels affecting treatment processes or changes in influent characteristics—our ability to meet permitted discharge and reuse standards could be compromised. This could lead to increased operational costs, production interruptions, enforcement actions, or the need to temporarily supplement treated water with alternative sources.

While we invest in monitoring and maintenance and maintain contingency plans, we cannot predict whether future local hydrologic conditions will be within design parameters. Any inability to operate treatment and reuse systems effectively could result in material adverse impacts to our operations and costs.

Our risk management efforts are designed to reduce the likelihood of disruptions, but the impact of natural variability and regulatory responses remains uncertain.

Accordingly, we cannot guarantee that our stormwater and erosion controls will be sufficient under all future conditions.

In addition, remediation can affect property values and may limit our ability to use or sell certain real estate.

We may also incur legal and consulting expenses associated with dispute resolution, and our insurance coverage may be limited by deductibles, coverage exclusions, or disputes regarding causation. Any significant adverse determination could have a material effect on our results of operations and liquidity.

Aging pipes, capacity constraints, and operational failures can increase the likelihood of water interruptions or reductions in water pressure and quality. Even if our internal facilities are capable of processing water, we may be impacted by external disruptions, including temporary loss of water supply or changes in treated water chemistry that require process adjustments.

In regions where water is shared among industrial users and public communities, utilities may ration supplies during periods of scarcity. If we are prioritized lower than other users or if regulators impose allocation priorities, our operations could be constrained. 

Our mitigation efforts include maintaining water storage capacity and backup treatment capability at certain sites. However, storage capacity can be limited, backup systems may not handle extreme conditions for extended periods, and additional reliance on alternative suppliers could increase operating costs. 

Because the performance of third-party water infrastructure is outside our control, disruptions to water availability and quality could materially affect our production, logistics, and overall operating expenses.

risk_heading: Water Stress and Availability Could Disrupt Our Operations

If water shortages were to occur, we may be required to reduce output, modify production schedules, or incur substantial costs to secure alternative water supplies, such as trucking, purchasing water from third parties, or investing in additional treatment and recycling systems. We also rely on water to maintain product quality and to meet environmental permits; inability to meet permit requirements due to limited water availability could result in enforcement actions or additional capital expenditures.

In addition, changes in water quality—such as increased salinity, contaminants, or temperature—could impair the performance of our equipment or products and may increase our operating costs. Even when alternative sources are available, they may be more expensive or may require new permits and infrastructure. Any significant disruption to water supply, including from prolonged drought or stricter water-use regulations, could adversely affect our business, results of operations, and financial condition.

Coastal resource constraints can be compounded by limitations on environmental permits, which may be influenced by habitat health and the presence of protected species. If mitigation requirements are imposed or if permits are delayed due to environmental review, our capital projects and operating timelines could be affected.

Any material damage from coastal impacts, inability to obtain or renew coastal permits, or significant costs associated with wetland restoration and mitigation could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.

risk_heading: Raw Material Sourcing From Sensitive Regions Could Be Constrained by Land and Ecosystem Protection Rules

Any sustained inability to obtain land-compliant raw materials could adversely impact our manufacturing, customer commitments, and financial results.

risk_heading: Failure to Protect Wetlands and Waterways May Result in Permit Denials or Enforcement

risk_heading: Climate-Related Changes to Groundwater Levels Could Disrupt Our Supply Chain
paragraph_text:

Groundwater levels can fluctuate due to prolonged drought, increased extraction, or changes in recharge rates. Where suppliers draw from aquifers, reduced availability can lead to pumping restrictions, higher extraction costs, or the need to source water from alternative systems.

If one or more key suppliers experience groundwater depletion or regulatory limits on well usage, they may reduce output or require longer lead times to procure water. These disruptions could propagate to us through shortages of intermediate inputs, altered product specifications, or increased prices. We may also be required to adopt different supplier standards to address variability in water availability or water chemistry.

Although we work with suppliers to encourage water-stewardship practices, our contractual leverage may not be sufficient to ensure continuity under rapidly worsening conditions. Additionally, suppliers may face community pressure or litigation related to local water impacts.

A significant disruption in the supply chain due to groundwater changes could adversely affect production schedules, customer service levels, and profitability.

risk_heading: Breach of Contractual Water-Stewardship Commitments Could Trigger Costly Remediation Measures
paragraph_text:

These commitments are often incorporated into customer contracts, permits, or sustainability agreements. If we fail to meet monitoring, reporting, or operational benchmarks, we could be required to undertake corrective action plans within prescribed timelines.

Corrective measures may include upgrading pumps or cooling systems, increasing recycling of process water, changing operational schedules to reduce withdrawal impacts during low-flow periods, or funding mitigation actions with third parties. Regulators may also require additional reporting or impose restrictions on future withdrawals if monitoring results demonstrate adverse impacts.

In addition, our ability to comply could be affected by factors outside our control, including changes in local hydrology, utility constraints, or upstream water-quality conditions that influence treatment requirements. If we experience unexpected downtime or failure of water-related infrastructure, we may temporarily increase water withdrawals or discharges, which could lead to non-compliance.

Any failure to comply with water-stewardship commitments could result in financial penalties, increased operating costs, reputational harm, and operational disruptions.

risk_heading: Restrictions on Land Development and Drainage Improvements Could Delay Infrastructure Updates

In some jurisdictions, local authorities may require the preservation of natural drainage patterns, limits on impervious surfaces, and compensatory measures for changes to runoff.

As regulators adopt more stringent requirements, the design and cost of our upgrades may increase, and approvals may take longer. In addition, if soil conditions are found to be less stable than anticipated or if the projects are located in areas with sensitive groundwater or ecological features, further studies and remediation may be required.

Our contractors may also be subject to evolving best practices for land management, and noncompliance could result in stop-work orders or additional mitigation. Delays in infrastructure updates can reduce operational efficiency, affect our ability to meet customer demand, and increase maintenance costs.

If we are unable to complete required land and drainage approvals on a timely basis or within budget, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Changes in Fishery and Aquatic Ecosystem Conditions Could Affect Our Seafood Ingredients
paragraph_text:

Our ability to source consistent quantities and quality may be influenced by changes in aquatic ecosystems, including water temperature shifts, harmful algal blooms, altered salinity, and declines in fish stocks. These conditions can result from environmental variability and long-term changes in climate and ecosystem health.

In addition, governments may implement new fishing quotas, seasonal closures, or gear restrictions intended to protect aquatic biodiversity and recover depleted stocks. Where these measures are adopted, our suppliers may not be able to procure adequate volumes at commercially reasonable prices or may be forced to substitute products with different characteristics.

We may also face challenges if environmental events lead to contamination concerns that require suppliers to discard harvests or impose stricter quality screening. While our quality assurance procedures are designed to reduce the risk of nonconforming ingredients, shortages and substitutions can increase costs and disrupt manufacturing schedules.

If fishery restrictions or ecosystem changes materially reduce the availability or quality of our seafood inputs, we may experience higher input costs, delays in production, and decreased ability to satisfy customer demand.

risk_heading: Changes in Permitted Water Withdrawal Volumes Could Require Costly Process Redesign

As a result, our future permitted withdrawal volumes may be lower than current levels or subject to stricter seasonal limitations.

If permitted volumes are reduced, we may need to redesign processes, install additional water-reuse systems, increase storage capacity, or shift production schedules to periods when withdrawals are allowed. Even if the required permits are obtained, the time required for installation and validation could affect our ability to meet customer delivery commitments.

In addition, compliance may require more frequent monitoring and reporting. If our measurement systems are not sufficiently accurate or if we experience operational upsets that lead to deviations from permit conditions, we may incur penalties or be required to implement corrective actions.

Any reduction in permitted water withdrawals, or the inability to implement timely process changes to operate within new limits, could adversely affect our operations, costs, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Erosion and Sedimentation at Our Sites Could Require Ongoing Land Restoration
paragraph_text:
Our facilities are subject to erosion and sedimentation risks due to rainfall patterns, storm runoff, and changes in surrounding land conditions. While we maintain control measures designed to limit soil movement, severe weather events can overwhelm drainage systems and increase sediment loads in nearby areas. These conditions can also degrade operational access roads and storage pads.

If erosion control measures do not perform adequately, we could face regulatory inquiries or be required to implement additional mitigation measures. Remedies may include regrading land, installing supplemental erosion barriers, stabilizing slopes, and undertaking sediment removal or revegetation. Such work may require permits and can disrupt operations.

Further, changes in the timing and intensity of rainfall can increase the frequency of events that trigger corrective actions. In addition, new land use developments in the vicinity of our properties could alter runoff patterns, potentially increasing erosion risks on our sites.

Any substantial increase in erosion-related incidents, costs to implement corrective actions, or inability to restore land to regulatory expectations could adversely affect our operating expenses and the ability to maintain our facilities.

risk_heading: Failure to Maintain Sustainable Forestry Practices Could Disrupt Wood-Based Supply

In parallel, regulators and customers may impose or update requirements relating to sustainable forestry practices, chain-of-custody documentation, and protection of critical habitats.

If suppliers are unable to secure timber that meets documentation and sustainability requirements, we may need to source from alternative suppliers or substitute other materials. While we maintain supplier qualification processes and contractual terms designed to reduce continuity risk, we cannot guarantee that these measures will be sufficient.

Any material disruption in access to compliant, sustainably harvested forestry inputs could adversely affect our production and financial results.

risk_heading: Misestimation of Environmental Impacts Could Lead to Additional Mitigation Costs
paragraph_text:

These assessments are based on available data and assumptions at the time they are prepared. However, conditions on the ground may change, including seasonal species presence, groundwater characteristics, and hydrologic response to nearby developments.

If subsequent surveys or regulatory reviews identify impacts that were not anticipated, permitting agencies may require additional mitigation measures beyond those originally contemplated. Mitigation can include habitat restoration, long-term monitoring, changes to construction sequencing, or establishment of additional buffers. These requirements can increase costs and delay construction schedules.

Environmental assessments may also be challenged by stakeholders, which can extend public comment periods or trigger additional review. If such reviews require new studies, we may need to pause or modify project activities.

Although we intend to comply with permit conditions and to update assessments when necessary, there is no assurance that mitigation costs will remain within budgeted amounts. Significant additional mitigation obligations could materially adversely affect our cash flows, capital expenditures, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Water Availability and Quality Risk
paragraph_text:
Our operations, including manufacturing, cooling, and cleaning processes, require access to reliable supplies of water. In certain regions where we operate, local authorities and water providers have signaled increased variability in precipitation, higher temperatures, and longer dry periods that can strain municipal and industrial supplies. In addition, water quality can be adversely affected by upstream discharges, aging infrastructure, or extreme weather events that cause sedimentation and contamination. If water becomes unavailable on commercially reasonable terms, or if the quality of water we receive fails to meet internal and regulatory specifications, we may be required to curtail production, install costly treatment systems, or secure alternative sources, such as trucking or supplemental wells, which may be unavailable during drought restrictions.

These outcomes could increase operating costs, reduce throughput, delay shipments, and require additional capital expenditures. While we maintain water management plans and conduct periodic testing, our mitigation efforts may not fully offset the impact of prolonged drought, regulatory changes to discharge permits, or the loss of supplier capacity in water-stressed areas.

If biodiversity risks increase or if suppliers face operational interruptions due to ecosystem-related disruptions, our supply of raw materials could be constrained, and we may incur increased costs to secure compliant alternatives.

risk_heading: Land Remediation and Environmental Liability Risk

Contamination may involve soil or groundwater impacts associated with fuels, solvents, and other materials historically used in operations. Even when we believe our practices comply with applicable laws, assessments can reveal previously unknown conditions or contamination levels that require additional investigation or remediation.

Remediation liabilities are often difficult to quantify because the scope of work depends on technical studies, changing regulatory requirements, and progress toward cleanup benchmarks. In certain jurisdictions, the identity and financial responsibility of potentially responsible parties can be disputed, resulting in uncertainty regarding cost allocations and timelines. Costs may include long-term monitoring, engineering controls, and restrictions on future use of the affected property.

If environmental conditions at a site require more extensive remediation than anticipated, or if we are deemed responsible for contamination beyond our expectations, our financial condition could be adversely affected through higher operating expenses, additional capital expenditures, and potential limits on property utilization.

Natural hazards can disrupt operations, degrade storage capacity, and increase downtime for maintenance and logistics. These regulatory and remediation requirements may be costly and could delay projects.

We attempt to design and maintain resilient infrastructure; however, our investments may not adequately address the frequency or severity of extreme weather events. If flooding or erosion causes damage that exceeds insurance coverage or requires extended remediation, our operating results and liquidity may be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Supply Constraints Due to Soil Degradation and Crop Volatility
paragraph_text:
Certain inputs used in our production depend on agricultural cultivation and the health of surrounding soils. Soil degradation caused by erosion, nutrient depletion, salinization, or excessive cultivation can reduce yields and quality, thereby increasing our exposure to shortages and price volatility. Soil conditions can deteriorate over time due to environmental factors, including changes in precipitation patterns, extreme heat, and improper land management by suppliers. When yields decline, suppliers may prioritize other buyers, restructure planting schedules, or substitute crops, which can impair continuity of supply.

We mitigate these risks by sourcing from multiple regions, using qualified suppliers, and contracting for specified agronomic practices; however, these measures do not guarantee stable yields. Some practices, such as improved irrigation efficiency, cover cropping, and soil-amending treatments, may require upfront investment that suppliers may not be able to fund without incentives or technical support. Additionally, multi-year growing cycles can delay recovery after a major adverse event.

If soil degradation accelerates or if crop volatility worsens, we may face higher raw-material costs, constrained volumes, and potential disruptions to manufacturing schedules, which could adversely affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Groundwater Withdrawal Limitations and Associated Costs
paragraph_text:
Some of our facilities rely on groundwater withdrawals to support certain processing and cooling requirements. Regulatory agencies in certain jurisdictions have increasingly imposed limits on groundwater extraction, require metering and reporting, and may revise permitted withdrawal volumes in response to declining aquifers or water-basin conditions. If permitted volumes are reduced, we may need to increase purchases from municipal utilities, invest in recirculation systems, or incur additional costs to operate with lower withdrawal levels.

Groundwater restrictions could also affect our ability to maintain production during peak demand periods or during seasonal variations. In addition, monitoring requirements could expand, requiring additional sampling, data management, and independent third-party verification. Non-compliance, even if inadvertent, can result in enforcement actions, penalties, or permit suspension, which may cause operational interruptions.

While we track withdrawals and work with consultants to assess groundwater conditions, the long-term sustainability of aquifers and the actions of regulatory authorities are uncertain. A reduction in permitted withdrawals could adversely affect our cost structure and operational reliability.

risk_heading: Risk Associated With Mineral Sourcing From Depleted or Scarce Resources
paragraph_text:
We source certain minerals and metals from regions facing resource depletion, changing extraction conditions, and constraints in nearby water and land systems that support mining operations. As accessible ore bodies decline, suppliers may need to increase stripping ratios, extend mine life infrastructure, or undertake remediation of disturbed land to maintain compliance. In extreme cases, mining operations can be suspended when water availability changes, when slope stability is compromised, or when remediation requirements cannot be met in a timely manner.

Customers and downstream counterparties increasingly request assurance that mineral supply chains do not contribute to significant land degradation or other ecosystem impacts. If suppliers cannot provide documentation, or if our due diligence identifies material gaps, we may need to switch to alternative suppliers that may have different specifications or higher costs. Such changes could also affect our ability to maintain consistent product quality.

Although we conduct supplier assessments and establish procurement standards, we cannot control the pace of environmental remediation by third parties or the operational resilience of their sites. Any material disruptions in mineral supply or increases in costs associated with land and resource constraints could adversely affect our results of operations.

risk_heading: Natural Disaster Impacts on Agricultural and Packaging Supply Chains
paragraph_text:
Our distribution and product fulfillment depend in part on agricultural and packaging supply chains that are vulnerable to natural disasters. Hurricanes, severe storms, and prolonged drought can damage crops used to produce certain paper, fiber, and bio-based packaging materials. Storms can also disrupt transportation networks and port operations, delaying inbound raw materials and outbound finished goods.

In addition, natural disasters can cause temporary closures of mills and manufacturing plants, which may lead to backlogs and reduced availability of specific product grades. Even if our suppliers resume operations, a recovery period may be required to restore equipment and inventory, during which we may be forced to accept alternative materials or requalify packaging to meet our specifications.

We attempt to reduce exposure through inventory management, dual-sourcing, and contracts that provide for allocation during disruptions. However, suppliers may prioritize other customers, and our ability to secure substitutes may be limited by the availability of equivalent materials after major weather events.

If disruptions persist, we may experience shortages, higher costs, and delayed shipments that could adversely affect customer relationships and operating results.

risk_heading: Increased Costs From Water and Land Conservation Measures at Sites

While these measures are intended to manage natural resources, they can increase costs and operational complexity. For example, we may need to retrofit equipment to reduce freshwater consumption, alter landscaping practices, and adjust maintenance routines to minimize water use.

Conservation actions can also affect how we manage stormwater and runoff on our sites. If conservation plans require changes in site drainage, detention capacity, or vegetation cover, we could incur costs to redesign site infrastructure and to conduct ongoing inspections to demonstrate compliance. These measures may also require coordination with third parties such as property managers and utilities.

Although we strive to anticipate regulatory and operational changes, conservation requirements may change without notice or may be tightened during drought emergencies. If we are unable to implement required measures on a timely basis, we could face enforcement actions or operational interruptions, which would adversely affect our results.

risk_heading: Risk of Reduced Availability of Reclaimed Water for Industrial Use
paragraph_text:
Some of our facilities use reclaimed or treated water provided by local utilities for non-potable applications, including equipment cooling and landscape uses. The availability and reliability of reclaimed water can be affected by fluctuations in incoming wastewater volumes, treatment capacity upgrades, and changes in regulatory standards for reclaimed water quality. In addition, utilities may reprioritize resources during drought conditions or infrastructure emergencies.

If reclaimed water supplies are curtailed or fail quality requirements, we may be required to switch to alternative sources, such as potable water or groundwater, which could be more expensive and subject to additional permits and restrictions. Switching may also require equipment adjustments and operational testing, which can temporarily reduce production efficiency.

We maintain contingency planning and monitor supplier quality reports; however, utility infrastructure decisions and third-party operational constraints are outside our control. Any sustained reduction in reclaimed water availability could increase operating costs, reduce throughput, and adversely affect our ability to meet customer delivery commitments.

In some cases, regulatory agencies require remediation to achieve specific land-use criteria, which may include limits on groundwater migration, soil vapor considerations, or ongoing monitoring obligations. If remediation work is delayed or extended due to technical constraints, we could face higher remediation expenses, tenant deferrals, or inability to utilize the parcel as planned.

Our due diligence processes are designed to identify known risks, but they may not fully capture all subsurface conditions or future regulatory interpretations. risk_heading: Impact of Reduced Fish Stocks or Waterway Health on Sourcing
paragraph_text:
Certain inputs in our supply chain rely on natural resources obtained from waterways, including fish and related aquatic materials. The productivity of these resources is influenced by water quality, temperature, oxygen levels, and habitat conditions. Changes in waterway health due to algal blooms, sedimentation, or upstream land-use activities can reduce the availability of target species and impair harvest yields. Additionally, extreme weather can disrupt migration patterns and increase the frequency of closures to protect depleted stocks.

We rely on third-party harvesters and processors, and our ability to substitute alternative sources may be limited by seasonality, quotas, and the requirement that suppliers meet specific quality and traceability standards. If harvest volumes decline, pricing can increase materially and delivery schedules can shift. We also may need to adjust product formulations or packaging specifications if alternative aquatic inputs do not meet our performance and safety standards.

While we maintain supplier contracts and perform traceability checks, we cannot control underlying environmental conditions. A sustained deterioration in waterway health or continued restrictions on harvesting could adversely affect our supply availability, cost structure, and ability to meet customer demand.

risk_heading: Risks From Environmental Changes Affecting Facility Cooling Systems

Our operations use water for certain cooling requirements and may draw from local water bodies or rely on municipal supplies. Environmental changes such as higher ambient temperatures, lower seasonal water levels, and altered water temperatures can reduce cooling system performance and increase the risk of non-routine operating conditions. If water intake temperatures exceed permitted thresholds or if water levels fall below operational limits, we could be required to reduce operating rates or install supplemental cooling capacity.

We also face constraints when local authorities impose temporary restrictions during periods of low water availability. These restrictions may limit both the volume of water used and the timing of withdrawals, which can impact production planning. In addition, changing water temperatures can increase scaling and maintenance needs, which would raise operating expenses.

We maintain cooling system maintenance and monitoring programs designed to manage known conditions; however, the magnitude and duration of environmental changes affecting intake and supply may exceed our forecasts. If cooling limitations cause sustained downtime or require additional capital expenditures, our results of operations could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Biodiversity and habitat impacts from land management activities may lead to project delays and additional remediation costs
paragraph_text:
Our operations and expansion plans require land use decisions and can affect nearby natural habitats, including wetlands, forests, and other sensitive ecological areas. Environmental conditions may be subject to change due to invasive species, weather variability, and shifting ecosystems, which can increase uncertainty around baseline biodiversity conditions and the effectiveness of mitigation measures. We conduct environmental assessments and implement habitat conservation or restoration plans where required, but these efforts may not fully prevent adverse impacts.

In some jurisdictions, permitting and approvals may depend on achieving specific conservation outcomes, meeting seasonal survey requirements, or demonstrating that mitigation offsets are sufficient. These changes could delay construction, increase operating costs, and reduce the expected return on capital.

Additionally, if land disturbances result in soil erosion, degradation of watercourses, or contamination migration, we may face remediation obligations. Remediation and ongoing monitoring could be costly and could extend over multiple years, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Remediation obligations for legacy site contamination could increase our liabilities and cash requirements
paragraph_text:
We are subject to environmental laws and regulations governing contamination and remediation at current and historical facilities, including requirements to investigate, remediate, and monitor contaminated soil and groundwater. Even where we have obtained permits or conducted prior remediation, contamination can migrate over time due to changes in hydrology, construction activities, or deterioration of containment systems. In addition, investigation results may reveal previously unknown contamination sources, including materials handled by prior owners or operators.

Remediation can involve excavation, treatment, removal of impacted media, and long-term groundwater monitoring. The scope and cost of required work are often difficult to estimate because they depend on site-specific conditions and regulatory determinations. Governmental authorities may change cleanup standards, require additional remedial actions, or increase oversight efforts, which could expand the duration and cost of cleanup.

We may also be required to contribute to remediation costs at off-site locations or third-party sites under environmental allocation arrangements. If our reserves are insufficient, we could incur material charges, face restrictions on future construction or operations, or be unable to fund remediation in a timely manner. Any significant remediation expense or delay in achieving closure could adversely affect our financial condition, results of operations, and liquidity.

risk_heading: Wastewater and Emissions Impacts of Facility Expansions
paragraph_text: When we expand or modify manufacturing lines, we must obtain permits and demonstrate that new equipment will not violate environmental limits related to air emissions and wastewater discharges. While we plan expansions with permitting timelines and engineering studies, construction schedules, commissioning delays, or changes to operating conditions can increase the risk of temporary noncompliance during startup. Startups can generate higher waste volumes, intermittent releases and unanticipated chemical concentrations in discharge streams. If operational tuning does not occur within expected time frames, we could exceed permitted limits or fail to meet reporting obligations, which could lead to enforcement actions or requirements to implement additional controls. Modifications may also increase the volume and complexity of solid and hazardous waste generated, requiring updates to waste handling permits and disposal contracting. In some cases, permits for expansions may include conditions that limit throughput or require monitoring that increases operating costs. Any delays or adverse permit outcomes could affect our ability to meet customer demand and increase our overall compliance costs.

risk_heading: Disposal of Spent Filters, Absorbents and Treatment Media
paragraph_text: Our pollution control systems, including filtration and activated media used to capture contaminants from wastewater and exhaust streams, generate spent materials that must be disposed of or recycled. The classification of these spent filters and treatment media depends on the captured contaminants, and their composition may vary based on operating conditions and upstream feedstock characteristics. If the material is found to be hazardous, disposal requires specialized handling and permitted facilities, which can be expensive and constrained by availability. Even when treated as non-hazardous, changes in regulatory thresholds or in sampling results could lead to reclassification and higher disposal costs. We rely on third-party facilities to accept and process spent media, and those facilities may reject loads that fail acceptance criteria, resulting in replacement costs and potential storage issues at our sites. Additionally, storage of spent media is time-limited under certain permits, and any delays could lead to compliance violations. The costs associated with proper disposal and any reclassification events may be material to our operating expenses.

risk_heading: Potential Product-Related Contaminant Release and Waste Generation
paragraph_text: Although our products are designed to meet applicable quality and safety standards, certain manufacturing processes and packaging steps involve materials that, if improperly handled, could lead to contamination during use or disposal by downstream parties. For example, defective seal integrity or improper curing in certain product components could cause trace contaminants to leach under specific conditions, creating health and environmental concerns for end users. If contamination is identified through customer reports or testing, we may be required to initiate containment actions, recall affected batches, and dispose of inventory and packaging materials that can become regulated waste. Such recalls could also require specialized disposal of returns and cleaning of customer premises, increasing costs. Additionally, our packaging design may influence how materials are disposed of; nonconforming labeling, incompatible packaging materials or damaged protective components can lead to increased waste and potential mismanagement by recyclers. While these risks are mitigated through quality controls, they cannot be eliminated. Any contamination incident that results in environmental cleanup, disposal liabilities, or recalls could adversely affect our financial results.

risk_heading: Environmental Compliance and Waste Handling Risks
paragraph_text:
Our manufacturing activities generate wastewater, air emissions, and waste streams that include materials that may be regulated as hazardous or non-hazardous waste, depending on their chemical composition and source. We use a combination of engineered controls, operating procedures, and licensed contractors to manage these waste streams, but we cannot assure that our practices will always prevent releases, misclassification, or disposal errors. Even minor spills, leaks, or container labeling failures can result in remediation costs, regulatory penalties, and third-party claims, including claims related to soil or groundwater contamination.

In addition, environmental regulations can change or be interpreted more restrictively. New requirements may increase the cost of treatment, storage, transportation, manifesting, and disposal, and may require additional capital investment in filtration, monitoring, and waste recovery systems. We also face uncertainty regarding the long-term stability and performance of treatment residues and recycled materials, which may be subject to reclassification over time. If we are required to remove or reprocess waste products at greater cost than anticipated, our results of operations could be adversely affected.

risk_heading: Risks Related to Lead, Solvent, and Other Hazardous Substances
paragraph_text:
We use and manage chemical substances in our operations, including metals, solvents, and catalysts that may be toxic, corrosive, or persistent in the environment if released. Although we maintain safety and environmental programs and train employees, the risk of contamination or injury from hazardous materials cannot be eliminated. Contamination may occur due to equipment failures, human error, or contractor performance, and such events can lead to contamination of air, stormwater systems, or soil.

We are subject to federal, state, and local requirements governing storage, handling, labeling, reporting, and disposal of hazardous substances. Compliance also includes tracking waste determinations and ensuring that waste is delivered to authorized facilities under applicable manifests and contracts. If we fail to satisfy these obligations, regulators could impose fines, corrective action requirements, or permit modifications that increase operating costs.

In certain instances, we may be required to remediate historical contamination at our sites or at properties we have used through prior operations or business acquisitions. The scope, timing, and cost of remediation are uncertain and depend on future investigative results and regulatory determinations. Any significant remediation or liability could adversely affect our financial condition and operating results.

risk_heading: Stormwater Discharges and Permit Violations
paragraph_text:
Our industrial facilities operate under environmental permits that govern discharges to waterways and requirements for handling and preventing releases during rainfall events. Even with stormwater best practices and containment measures, weather conditions, equipment downtime, and construction activities can increase the likelihood of discharges, exceedances, or permit violations. Regulatory agencies may require investigations and may impose penalties for noncompliance, including costs related to sampling, monitoring, and remediation.

Permits may also be renewed with more stringent limits on parameters such as chemical oxygen demand, suspended solids, metals, or pH. Additionally, interpretations of water quality standards may change over time. If we are unable to modify our operating systems or treatment methods on a timely basis, we could incur higher operating costs and potential shutdowns while corrective actions are implemented.

We may also become responsible for environmental liabilities associated with releases originating from third-party contractors or neighboring properties. Any such incidents could result in government enforcement actions and claims from others, which may not be fully covered by insurance or indemnities. Adverse outcomes could materially impact our results of operations.

risk_heading: Recycling, Packaging, and Producer Responsibility Obligations
paragraph_text:
We sell consumer and commercial products in markets where producer responsibility and packaging regulations may require collection, recycling, or reporting of packaging materials. These obligations can change quickly as jurisdictions adopt new extended producer responsibility frameworks or revise recycling targets. Although we work with logistics and recycling partners, the performance of collection and recycling systems depends on third parties over whom we have limited control.

Our compliance costs may increase due to higher fees for recycling services, changes to reporting requirements, constraints on which packaging formats are accepted for recycling, and the need to redesign packaging to meet local rules. If packaging is deemed noncompliant or if reporting data submitted to regulators is found to be inaccurate, we could face fines, corrective action requirements, or required refunds of fees.

Moreover, recycling markets are dynamic. If recyclers experience capacity constraints or contamination levels rise, the value and availability of recycled materials we use in our packaging or manufacturing may decline. In some cases, we may be required to use alternative materials that are more expensive or that do not perform as expected. Any of these developments could increase operating costs and adversely affect margins.

risk_heading: Hazardous Air Emissions and Operational Exceedances
paragraph_text:
We operate facilities that are subject to air quality regulations covering emissions of pollutants such as volatile organic compounds, particulates, nitrogen oxides, and other hazardous air contaminants. Emissions limits are set through permits and applicable standards, and compliance depends on the proper functioning of control equipment, accurate monitoring, and adherence to operating conditions. Abnormal operating events, maintenance issues, or feedstock variability can result in short-term exceedances.

If we exceed emissions limits, regulators may require submission of deviation reports, corrective action plans, additional monitoring, and in some cases the payment of civil penalties. Repeat or significant violations can also lead to permit suspension or modification, potentially constraining production. We also could be subject to citizen suits alleging violations of permits or statutory requirements.

Further, air regulations may be tightened, including requirements to use cleaner fuels, improve capture efficiencies, or reduce emissions from equipment such as boilers and process units. Implementing these changes may require capital expenditures and downtime for upgrades.

We may not be able to predict the timing or cost of such compliance efforts, and any failure to achieve or sustain compliance could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, and financial condition.

risk_heading: Contamination Liability from Past Waste Disposal Practices
paragraph_text:
We could incur environmental liabilities related to contamination at current or historical properties. Some of our sites and equipment have been in operation for many years, and certain waste handling practices used in prior periods may not meet current standards. In addition, sites used by predecessors or former operators may present contamination risks that can extend beyond the boundaries of our properties.

Under environmental laws, liability for cleanup and damages may apply regardless of fault, and liability can include costs for investigation, remediation, monitoring, and long-term management of contaminated materials. It is difficult to predict the timing, scope, or total cost of remediation, particularly where regulators require additional sampling or where conditions such as soil composition and groundwater flow create uncertainty.

We could also face claims from third parties, including landowners or neighboring businesses, alleging property damage or exposure to hazardous substances. The outcome of any investigation or enforcement action is inherently uncertain, and we may need to reserve additional amounts or incur cash expenditures that are not fully covered by insurance.

Any significant contamination liability could adversely affect our liquidity and financial condition.

risk_heading: E-Waste Takeback and Storage Compliance Risks
paragraph_text:
We provide product takeback and end-of-life services for certain electronics sold in jurisdictions that impose e-waste requirements. Our obligations may include collection coordination, inspection of returned units, storage of components, and transfer to certified recyclers. Returned products may contain batteries, capacitors, or circuit boards with hazardous constituents. If items are mishandled, damaged during storage, or processed by recyclers that do not meet regulatory standards, we may face compliance and environmental release risks.

The requirements also evolve. Regulatory authorities may expand the scope of covered products, tighten permitted storage conditions, or require more detailed reporting on recycling outcomes. We must maintain accurate records of serial numbers, weights, and disposition pathways to support required disclosures. Any errors in reporting or documentation could lead to enforcement actions.

In addition, recycled material markets can change, affecting the economics of takeback programs and the level of recovered value. We may need to adjust takeback volumes, refine sorting procedures, or revise contracts with recyclers to ensure compliance. If we are unable to manage these factors, costs could increase and our operations could be adversely impacted.

risk_heading: Waste Transport, Contractor, and Manifesting Risks
paragraph_text:
A portion of our environmental compliance relies on third-party waste haulers and disposal facilities to transport and treat materials generated in our operations. While we select licensed vendors and require contractual environmental standards, we do not control the day-to-day activities of these third parties. Failures in waste handling—such as improper loading, unauthorized dumping, incomplete manifests, or storage beyond permitted timeframes—can create regulatory exposure and potential environmental harm.

Waste may be classified differently by regulators or facilities, and changes to waste characterization can lead to delays and increased costs, including additional testing and re-submittal of waste profiles. If a waste stream is reclassified as hazardous, we may need to adjust disposal methods and carriers, potentially increasing disposal expenses and reducing availability.

In the event of a spill, fire, or release during transport or at a disposal facility, regulators may seek information about the generator, including our documentation, training, and procedures. Even where we are not at fault, we could be required to fund investigations or participate in remediation. Such costs may be material and could adversely affect our operating results.

risk_heading: Residue Management and Beneficial Reuse Uncertainty
paragraph_text:
Certain by-products and treatment residues generated by our processes may be eligible for beneficial reuse or recycling if they meet regulatory requirements. However, eligibility can depend on chemical properties, contaminant thresholds, and how the materials are used at end destinations. Regulators may require additional testing, impose conditions, or determine that a material is not eligible for reuse, in which case it would need to be handled as regulated waste.

Our ability to use residuals in customer applications or in our own operations may be affected by changing standards, inspection outcomes, or revisions to beneficial-use determinations. If a residue is reclassified or restricted, we may be forced to seek alternative disposal methods that are typically more expensive and may have limited capacity in certain geographic regions.

In addition, beneficial reuse programs can create downstream environmental risk if end users store, transport, or apply the residue improperly. Even when we provide documentation and specifications, we may not control the end use and storage practices of third parties. Adverse events could result in regulatory inquiries and claims for cleanup.

If beneficial reuse arrangements become unavailable or more costly, our waste management costs and overall operating expenses could increase materially.

risk_heading: Facility Upgrades for Effluent Treatment and Sludge Disposal
paragraph_text:
We discharge treated effluents from industrial processes through publicly regulated treatment systems or permitted outfalls. While our treatment systems are designed to remove regulated pollutants, the performance of effluent treatment can be affected by operating conditions, equipment reliability, and variability in influent characteristics. If treatment efficiency declines, we could exceed permit limits or have unauthorized discharges.

Many permits also require specific limits for persistent pollutants and periodic testing and reporting. Noncompliance could trigger enforcement actions, including required process modifications, increased monitoring, and administrative orders. We may also be required to reduce discharge volumes during certain periods.

Treatment generates sludge and other waste residuals that must be disposed of or stabilized in accordance with applicable regulations. Sludge handling can be expensive and may be subject to changing requirements based on waste characterization and contaminant levels. Limited availability of permitted disposal capacity could result in higher transportation and disposal costs.

In addition, the timeline and scope of facility upgrades are uncertain and depend on design, permitting, and contractor performance. If upgrades are delayed or costlier than expected, our operating costs and ability to meet contractual and regulatory commitments could be adversely impacted.

risk_heading: Battery Handling, Disposal, and Fire-Related Environmental Risks
paragraph_text:
We manage and store battery components and other materials that can present environmental and safety risks if damaged. Improper handling, defective packaging, or exposure to heat can cause battery swelling, leakage, or fires. Even when incidents are contained, they may release hazardous substances such as heavy metals and electrolytes, requiring specialized cleanup and disposal of contaminated debris.

Our sites maintain fire prevention systems and procedures for receiving, inspection, and staging of materials. However, we cannot assure that these controls will fully prevent incidents. In addition, the disposal of batteries and related waste streams is subject to stringent regulations regarding characterization, segregation, transport, and recycling. If waste is mischaracterized or if storage and packaging requirements are not met, regulators may impose penalties and require corrective action.

Fire and release events can also lead to unplanned downtime and increased costs for environmental contractors. Insurance coverage may not fully address all remediation, operational interruption, or third-party claims.

As battery technologies evolve and regulatory guidance changes, we may need to update storage configurations, training programs, and recycling contracts. Any failure to manage these risks could result in material costs and adverse effects on our results of operations.

We may also be required to conduct remedial investigations at sites where our current records are incomplete due to legacy operations.

In addition, recycling standards and exemptions may change, requiring us to alter sorting practices, sampling, or processing methods to qualify materials for recycling. These events could increase operating costs and cause production scheduling disruptions. While we attempt to maintain contractual and operational flexibility, we cannot ensure that recycling diversion targets will remain cost-effective under changing market and regulatory conditions.

risk_heading: Potential Liability for Releases of Pollutants from Aging Infrastructure

Even without confirmed releases, regulators may require corrective action based on inspection findings, which could increase capital expenditures. Any material infrastructure failure or regulatory action could adversely affect our financial condition and operating results.

risk_heading: Environmental Compliance and Hazardous Waste Management Risks

We could be required to invest in additional containment, treatment systems, or monitoring, and such costs may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

risk_heading: Wastewater Discharge Permit and Treatment System Failure Risks
paragraph_text:
We discharge or transfer process water and other wastewater streams generated by our facilities to permitted municipal systems or subject them to treatment prior to discharge. Our ability to operate within permit limits depends on the performance of treatment equipment, timely maintenance, and the quality of influent. If treatment systems experience mechanical failures, power interruptions, chemical supply disruptions, or unanticipated variability in wastewater composition, we could exceed discharge limits or cause unauthorized releases. Any such events could trigger notices of violation, fines, consent decrees, or required upgrades.

Regulatory requirements for wastewater are frequently updated, and agencies may impose more stringent effluent limits, monitoring frequency, or reporting obligations. Even when we take corrective actions, we may not be able to quickly reach compliance due to technology constraints, lead times for capital projects, or the need to modify production processes. In addition, we rely on third-party contractors and treatment facilities to handle certain sludges and residuals. Contractors’ failure to comply with hazardous waste or wastewater rules could expose us to liability.

Any enforcement activity or remediation costs could be material and may also disrupt operations, affecting customer supply and our operating results.

risk_heading: Air Emissions, Dust Control, and Solid Waste Disposal Compliance Risks

If equipment malfunctions, if operational upsets occur, or if feedstock or catalysts vary, we could exceed permit thresholds or fail to meet reporting requirements.

Our facilities are subject to complex permitting frameworks and operating limitations, and authorities may require additional controls in response to health-based standards, tighter ambient air targets, or updated interpretations of applicable rules. We also face risk from the disposal of residues and spent materials. Determinations by waste generators, regulators, or receiving facilities regarding whether a waste stream is hazardous may affect disposal costs and necessitate changes to handling procedures.

We may be required to invest in additional pollution-control systems, alternative disposal methods, or product/process redesigns to satisfy permit conditions. Any failure to comply, even if inadvertent, could result in penalties, injunctive relief, or forced downtime. These outcomes could materially adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations.

risk_heading: Recycling Program and Take-Back Obligation Costs for Electronic Components

The obligations vary by jurisdiction and may change as regulators update definitions of covered products, recycling targets, and reporting requirements.

Our recycling arrangements depend on third-party processors and recyclers. If a recycler is unable to perform in accordance with applicable environmental and safety requirements, or if it underreports the characterization of waste streams, we could face liability, higher costs, or the loss of capacity to meet our obligations. In addition, contamination in collected materials can reduce recycling yields and increase the volume of waste requiring landfill disposal or treatment as hazardous waste.

We estimate and accrue for recycling-related obligations based on historical volumes and expected costs. However, our assumptions may be inaccurate due to shifts in product mix, consumer behavior, resale and reuse patterns, changes in recycling technology, or regulatory enforcement. Material increases in recycling costs or enforcement actions related to compliance could adversely impact our results of operations.

risk_heading: Packaging Waste Reduction Requirements and Vendor Compliance

risk_heading: Evolving Rules for Hazardous Substances in Manufacturing Inputs

Regulations such as those addressing restricted chemicals and hazardous substances in products and waste can require changes to inputs, process controls, and documentation we provide to customers and recyclers.

Compliance relies on supplier disclosure, quality testing, and accurate documentation for each lot of materials. We may also be exposed to liability if chemicals are not properly managed at the end of a product’s lifecycle. For example, if certain constituents are not effectively removed during refurbishment, disposal vendors may classify waste differently, increasing disposal costs and compliance requirements.

Any inability to comply with restricted substance requirements or any associated disposal and redesign costs could materially affect our results of operations. Regulatory developments and enforcement priorities can also change quickly, making it difficult to accurately forecast costs and timing of compliance initiatives.

Material changes in the cost or availability of recycling or disposal routes for residuals could adversely affect our operating margins and liquidity.

risk_heading: E-Waste and Electronic Components Disposal Compliance Risks
paragraph_text:

Failure to meet e-waste obligations could result in regulatory investigations, civil penalties, and demands to remediate improperly managed waste. Our ability to manage these requirements may be affected by changes in permitted recycling technologies, evolving definitions of “hazardous” versus “non-hazardous” components, and variations in how rules are enforced across states. Furthermore, product returns can be difficult to predict, and volumes may increase rapidly after product upgrades or customer service campaigns.

These factors could increase our operating expenses and create reputational risks associated with improper waste handling.

risk_heading: Contaminated Materials and By-Product Handling May Trigger Enforcement Actions
paragraph_text:
Certain materials used in our processes can become contaminated with regulated substances and may require special handling, storage, and disposal. We operate production lines that create by-products, spent media, and filter residues that must be evaluated to determine whether they qualify as hazardous or non-hazardous waste under applicable rules. The determination of waste classification may change based on test results, regulatory guidance, or the interpretation of how contaminants should be measured and aggregated.

Although we employ sampling and testing programs, test results may be inconsistent due to variability in input materials, the limited representativeness of grab samples, or changes in operating conditions. As a result, materials that we previously treated as non-hazardous could later be determined to be hazardous, and vice versa. If waste is misclassified, disposed of improperly, or stored in a manner that does not meet permit or facility requirements, regulators could take enforcement actions.

Enforcement could include suspension or limitation of activities, required changes to waste handling practices, corrective actions, and substantial civil penalties. We may also be required to fund remediation of waste areas or to pay for replacement capacity if waste handling is disrupted.

These events could materially adversely affect our financial results and liquidity.

risk_heading: Spills and Waste Transport Incidents Could Result in Significant Remediation Costs
paragraph_text:
Our operations depend on the safe storage and transport of chemicals and waste materials to and from manufacturing and distribution sites. Despite training, standard operating procedures, and engineered containment measures, spills or releases may occur during transfer, loading, or transportation. Such incidents could involve chemical leaks, damaged containers, or losses resulting from extreme weather, traffic accidents, or unexpected equipment failures.

If a spill occurs, we may need to respond immediately, contain impacted areas, and coordinate investigation and cleanup activities. Depending on the materials released and the location of the incident, required remediation could include removal of contaminated soil, treatment of affected groundwater, air monitoring, and disposal of cleanup debris. Regulators may also require additional reporting, revise permit terms, or impose restrictions that reduce operational flexibility until corrective actions are completed.

We could face liability for cleanup costs and damages, including claims by customers, local communities, or third parties. We also rely on third-party carriers and waste management contractors; if they do not follow required procedures for packaging, handling, and documentation, incidents could occur for which we may nevertheless remain responsible.

A severe or repeated spill event could increase costs materially, disrupt operations, and lead to adverse legal outcomes.

risk_heading: Recycling Market and Take-Back Program Changes May Affect Waste Management Strategy
paragraph_text:
We participate in take-back and recycling arrangements for certain materials and products, including scrap generated in manufacturing and customer-returned components. Our waste management approach depends, in part, on the availability and pricing of recycling services and the ability of recycling facilities to accept relevant material streams that meet contract specifications. Recycling markets can be volatile and may be affected by changes in commodity prices, regulatory requirements for recyclers, and disruptions to collection logistics.

If recycling capacity declines or recyclers reduce acceptance of certain streams due to updated permitting standards or end-market constraints, we may need to manage materials through alternative disposal or treatment methods that are more expensive and may require longer lead times. In addition, contract requirements for documentation and residue handling may become more stringent, increasing administrative costs.

Regulatory agencies may also revise definitions regarding whether certain materials qualify for recycling versus disposal, and whether recycling residues are classified as hazardous waste. Misalignment between our classification approach and regulators’ expectations could result in enforcement, remediation, or penalties.

Because these factors are outside our control and can change quickly, we cannot predict the extent to which recycling and take-back program costs may increase. Such increases could adversely affect our results of operations.
